A good man with power can fix bad men with power for about 30 years or so. And even a good man usually grows more corrupt and detached over decades.

To more persistently fix a bad situation after defeating it historically requires putting in place a more durable institution that is not tied to a single, centralized, person. And that requires cultivating buy-in by the population to support that institution more-so than the person.

This goes all the way back to why humans and other apes are different. Apes recognize a singular ape as having power, which works at the scale of the jungle. Humans can abstract the position of the leader ape, the leader human, from the individual currently in charge, and ask what process should we follow for rulership and law in a long-term sense to inhabit that position. We have the mental capacity to separate the position from the person. What rules do we follow that are broader than one person, to lead to rulership from generation to generation?

Sometimes a key man is needed (or a woman, usually a man, let's say person) for change when things are dire. But what turns a temporary change into a durable institution is whether they can land the plane in a way that carries on beyond them.

Can they gain power and then distribute it? Can they become the ape that dominates the other apes and then separates himself from that position, so that what was built can continue on for centuries?

Most don't. Most continue the cycle of emerging markets that never emerge. Rarely, one bubbles to the top and manages it, in a context to more durably transfer leadership, transfer law, and signal to the world that the rule of law and rule of capital in their country isn't tied to one person but rather has a broader base to bet on. That base requires citizens to buy into it, and for their leaders to empower independent courts. It's less about one leader at that point, and more about whether the culture that let bad men come into power is now more durably able to put good men (and women) in power or not. What changed, culturally and legally? What was put in place to stop the cycle? To make the centralized power not tied to one mortal person, but rather able to transfer? What turned chaos into law for more than one lifetime?

The narrow path is to win decisively, and then help distribute the power, and teach the new culture. But few manage it. It's like rising to a George Washington level of domination and then gradually letting go.

Banks don't lend reserves. They lever reserves and make IOUs on top of them, rather than "creating money."

But then whenever those IOUs start to fail at scale, the central bank creates more reserves for them.

Over the past 50 years, if the US central bank held reserves flat and banks kept making money, there'd be a 160-to-1 ratio between deposits and reserves, which would be untenable. However, whenever it comes even slightly untenable, the central bank creates more reserves and swaps them for assets from banks, boosting the ratio and giving banks more lending/leveraging ability to keep it growing.

The US bank deposit-to-reserve ratio is under 4-to-1 because the central bank accommodates bank lending by creating new reserves.

US consumers are still spending despite historically low sentiment:

US retail sales jumped +0.8% in September, to a record $745 billion.

This follows a +1.3% gain in August and marks the 7th increase over the last 8 months.

Over the last 2 years, retail sales have risen +$69 billion, or +10%.

Meanwhile, US consumer sentiment fell -1.8 points in early October, to 46.3, its 2nd-lowest in history.

Sentiment deteriorated most among lower-income consumers and those with smaller stock market portfolios.

Over the last 2 years, consumer sentiment has fallen -23.8 points, or -34%.

The disconnect between what consumers think about the economy and how they spend is widening.

Excluding years when global EPS declined YoY, this would mark the 2nd-highest level of single-sector earnings concentration over the last 30 years, exceeded only during the 2022 energy crisis.

BREAKING: China’s central bank officially bought +26 tonnes of gold in October, its biggest monthly purchase since August 2023.

This follows +23 tonnes acquired in September, and marks its 24th consecutive month of gold purchases.

For perspective, in 2025, China’s gold purchases did not exceed +5 tonnes in any month.

Year-to-date, China has officially acquired +129 tonnes of gold, lifting its holdings to a record 2,435 tonnes.

As a result, China now holds just 2 tonnes less gold than France, the world’s 4th-largest gold holder.

China’s demand for gold shows no signs of slowing.

US hiring is showing no signs of a recovery.

New job postings on Indeed fell -4.8% YoY in the week ending October 16th.

Since April 2022, new job postings have now declined -46.7%.

As a result, the number of new available vacancies in the US is -0.8% below pre-pandemic levels recorded in February 2020.

Over the last several months, the pace of decline has slowed, but there have been no signs of a rebound in hiring either.

This suggests a lack of a significant recovery in official BLS job openings data, which lags job postings data by a few weeks.

The US labor market remains weak beneath the surface.

Nvidia is experiencing a historic losing streak:

Nvidia, $NVDA, has declined for 6 consecutive weeks, matching its 2nd-longest weekly losing streak on record.

Over this span, the stock has declined -31%, to its lowest level since July 2025.

Similar 6-week losing streaks occurred twice in 2012 and once in 2002, following the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble burst.

By comparison, its longest losing streak was7 weeks, recorded during the 2008 Financial Crisis when $NVDA dropped -53%.

Since its October peak, Nvidia has lost -$1.9 trillion in market value, down to $3.9 trillion.

Year-to-date, the stock is down -12%, materially underperforming the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, which are up +10% and +11%, respectively.

Nvidia is facing a nearly unprecedented downturn.

Investors are demanding more compensation for holding US tech debt:

US investment-grade (IG) technology bonds are underperforming the broader IG corporate bond market by -9% year-to-date.

This brings the total return of IG tech bonds relative to broader IG bonds down to its lowest level in at least 30 years.

At the same time, the difference between IG technology bond spreads over Treasuries and broader IG corporate bond spreads over Treasuries has widened to +15 basis points, the widest in at least 14 years.

By comparison, this difference was negative from 2012 through 2025.

In other words, investors are demanding a higher yield premium to hold technology debt than the broader IG corporate bond market.

This comes as Big Tech bond issuance has surged to a record $182 billion so far in 2026, up +971% from just $17 billion in 2024, making AI the largest sector in the IG bond market.

Financing the AI revolution is becoming more expensive.
